task: Use structured C++/Java acceptance comparisons to identify bounded semantic-checker gaps.
observation: A recursive differential command traversed 1,021 files because the harness recursively expands directory arguments. Its acceptance failures included overlapping WRITE/READ calls, immutable incoming payload use, ordinary recursion, concrete domain-route cycles, no-value method returns, spaced typed collection constructors, and project module loading of unrelated siblings. Focused reproductions isolated small fixes for the first groups and import-closure loading; a bounded top-level set then passed 41/41.
impact: Explicit file lists or top-level globs are important for controlling differential scope. The focused fixes add meaningful acceptance coverage without repeating generated-Rust comparisons. Remaining broader corpus cases show the current 41-file sample does not establish full semantic parity.

task: Close a focused structural-trait forwarding false rejection in Java semantic checking.
observation: RungeKutta's generic helper forwards a parameter constrained by DynamicalSystem to another function requiring DynamicalSystem. Java previously treated the trait-constrained actual as a concrete object and rejected the call. Exact same-trait forwarding is now accepted; a different trait constraint remains rejected. The full example then reaches a C++-only open-result diagnostic later, so this correction does not establish parity or native validity.
impact: Structural constraints must be preserved when a generic function forwards an argument under the same trait. Treating the constraint as a concrete nominal object creates false rejection; accepting a different trait would be unsound.

task: Reject false structural-trait satisfaction based on method name alone.
observation: A minimal `Readable` trait required `read(Int) -> Int`, while a concrete object exposed `read(String) -> Int`. C++ rejected the object as not satisfying the trait; Java previously checked only the method name and accepted it when the constrained argument was otherwise unused. Java now checks method arity and declared parameter and return types.
impact: Method-name-only checking can accept invalid structural types and produce later backend failures. Signature checking preserves the compile-time trait predicate.

task: Preserve inferred open result types for value-returning generic functions.
observation: A minimal `fn identity(value): return value` was accepted by both compilers, but Java semantic checking discarded the unresolved result variable and defaulted it to Unit after correctly inferring the parameter/result relationship. The checker now defaults an unresolved result to Unit only when the function has no value return, and retains resolved parameter checker TypeRefs separately from source annotations. A second regression calls the same identity function with Int and String; both call sites retain their distinct concrete specializations.
impact: This preserves the generic identity relationship in Java checker state without fabricating a source annotation or changing code generation. It establishes one focused generic semantic fact; broader generic inference and ABI summary production remain open.
